[PAPER_0025, relevance_score=0.395] Our main prediction, as specified in the preregistration, was that geminate spellings of final consonants would be more likely for content words than for function words. This result would point to part of speech as an influence on spelling. We also predicted that geminate responses would be more likely in the choice task than the production task. This result would support the task differences observed in Experiment 1 and in previous work (Hayes et al., 2006), showing that a preference for short, simple spellings is particularly likely in the effortful task of spelling production.

[PAPER_0026, relevance_score=0.334] A final prediction stemmed from the exploratory analysis in Experiment 1 that showed a higher rate of "other" responses to two-phoneme content words than to three-phoneme content words in the production task. This difference might reflect participants' attempts to lengthen their spellings of two-phoneme content words in ways other than or in addition to gemination of the final consonant.

[PAPER_0057, relevance_score=0.326] Supporting our main preregistered hypothesis, geminate responses were more common for content words than for function words. The main effect of task was also significant (b = 1.11, SE = 0.34, p = .001). Geminate responses were, as predicted, more likely to occur in the choice task than the production task. There was a tendency for the effect of syntactic category to be larger in the choice task than the production task, but the interaction between syntactic category and task was not statistically reliable (p = .09).

[PAPER_0062, relevance_score=0.269] The results of Experiment 1 suggested that participants in the production task sometimes used methods other than gemination of final consonants to lengthen the spellings of content words that would otherwise have two letters. Responses in the "other" category were less common in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1, for reasons that are unclear, and these responses were not more common for content words than for function words. The results of Experiment 2 do not support the hypothesis that "other" responses reflect attempts to lengthen spellings of content words by using methods other than final consonant gemination.
